summary.text: Traditional 別 is analyzed as a knife beside a bare-bone shape, depicting flesh being separated from bone. Modern 别 is used for “separate,” “other,” and “do not.”

formation.text: 別 is a semantic compound: the knife and bare-bone shape together depict cutting flesh from bone, suggesting separation. The bone shape is associated with 冎, though their precise graphic relationship is unresolved. The proposed 刂 + 另 analysis is not supported for the traditional graph.

components.text: The left element in traditional 別 is described as a bare-bone shape, contributing the bone in the cutting image. It is associated with 冎, but their exact graphic relationship is unresolved.
The right element in traditional 別 is 刂, the conventional side form of 刀, depicting a knife. The sources do not establish a complete sequence of graph shapes for 別.

history.text: Early graph descriptions show a knife beside a bare-bone shape; the transmitted analysis of 𠛰 gives 冎 plus 刀. The reported oracle-bone occurrence may be a place or sacrificial name, so it does not securely attest an ordinary cutting sense. Available accounts do not give a complete dated sequence leading to standard 別.

别 is connected with traditional 別, but it is not established as a straightforward stroke reduction. The 1956 standard pairs 别 with 彆; the earlier variant history connecting 别 with 別 remains unresolved.

uncertainties.text: The bone-and-knife construction is supported, but the precise graphic relationship among the early bone shape, 𠛰, and later 別 remains unresolved.

The origin of the prohibition sense “do not” is disputed. Proposals connect it with 不要 or 不必, or with an extension from “other/separate”; no single source or pathway is established for all modern uses.

senses.text: The proposed bone-and-knife interpretation suggests cutting apart, and later textual examples include physically separating or opening. The disputed oracle-bone occurrence does not securely attest this as the earliest written sense.
Historical phonological and textual discussions record an intransitive sense, “be separated.” Its chronology and relation to the transitive sense “separate” remain disputed.

senses.period: Warring States and Han examples reported; exact dates unresolved
senses.text: Reported manuscript examples use 別 for classifying and expressing distinctions. They attest those uses but do not establish a complete development from cutting apart.
“Other” is a recorded current sense. When and through what change it developed from separating or distinguishing remain unresolved.

senses.period: Yuan period proposed; prominence reported from Ming–Qing onward
senses.text: The prohibition sense is current. Proposed histories connect it with 不要, 不必, or an extension from “other/separate”; its source and proposed dating remain provisional.

developments.text: Cutting apart and being separated are related meanings, but the evidence does not establish their direction or a secure transition.
A development from parting to distinction is possible, but not established. Analyses of the intransitive and transitive readings also compete.
Extension from “other/separate” is one proposed explanation for the prohibition sense, alongside contraction accounts; it is not established.

limitations.text: The reported oracle-bone occurrence is disputed as a place or sacrificial name and cannot establish the earliest ordinary lexical sense. Examples and modern glosses alone do not establish the full chronology of meanings.
The origin and dating of the prohibition sense remain unresolved. The proposed Yuan and Ming–Qing chronology comes from research not fully accessible for verification.
